<reason>Both sides argued well, and the debate narrowed cleanly to the right question: what "prioritise" costs, and in what order clips get commissioned. CON landed the two sharpest hits of the debate — the "name the loser" pressure question, and the exploitation of PRO's floor ("even if she never learns who made it, that is relevance") as self-anonymising public money. But CON's route to victory depended on a dilemma it could not close. To make the tradeoff bite, CON redefined the motion's "traditional channel expansion" as owned distribution generally (on-demand app, kids' service, minority-language offer), which PRO correctly identified as smuggling standing commitments into a motion about expansion. Once CON conceded in [B4.7] that "nobody is" launching linear channels, and in [B4.3]/[B4.4] that the newsroom should make clips and publish them in feeds, PRO's load-bearing empirical claims (the young are not on the schedule; new channels reach only existing channel-watchers) stood essentially unrefuted, and the remaining dispute was ordering — where PRO's "afterthought clips get skipped, native ones get watched" plus the funk example is the more concrete mechanism, and CON's closing damage list (election night, minority-language, the four-part investigation) rests on a version of PRO's case PRO had already disavowed. PRO also handled pressure more honestly: it named the loser plainly and explicitly refused to invent an attribution statistic, then reframed the funnel as non-decisive rather than dodging. Grounding was disciplined on both sides (BBC Three, funk, the 2016 Facebook video pivot), with no fake precision. CON's "trust is carried into the clip, not created by it" and "you will compete on charisma against professional charismatics" were the best conceptual counters and keep this close, but PRO ends with the cleaner, motion-faithful comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's "name the loser" question and follow-up dilemma — either PRO means nothing (a phantom fifth channel) or it defunds the pensioner and the long investigation — was the most damaging single move, sharpened by its attack on PRO's [A4.5] floor as "relevance you cannot be credited for." PRO survived it by answering plainly (the loser is expansion), showing that CON's damage list consists of standing commitments the motion never ranks, and turning attribution back: content a generation never sees has an attribution rate of zero.</best_rebuttal>
